questions.question: Where must a super(...) call appear inside a constructor?
questions.explanation: The parent part of the object must be built before any child code runs, so super(...) has to come first.

questions.question: A child constructor contains no super(...) or this(...) call. What does the compiler do?
options: It inserts super() with no arguments
It reports an error every time
It calls the parent constructor with default values
questions.explanation: javac adds super() automatically. If the parent has no no-argument constructor, that inserted call fails to compile.

questions.question: class A { A() { System.out.print("A"); } } class B extends A { B() { System.out.print("B"); } } class C extends B { C() { System.out.print("C"); } } What does new C(); print?
questions.explanation: Each constructor first calls its parent's, so the bodies finish from the top of the tree down: A, then B, then C.

questions.question: class Car { String tag() { return "car"; } } class Ev extends Car { String tag() { return super.tag() + "+ev"; } } What does System.out.println(new Ev().tag()); print?
questions.explanation: super.tag() runs Car's version, which returns car, and the override appends +ev.

questions.question: class Car { Car(String model) { } } class Ev extends Car { Ev() { System.out.println("EV"); } } Why does Ev fail to compile?
options: println is not allowed in constructors
The inserted super() finds no no-argument constructor in Car
questions.explanation: Ev must call super("some model") explicitly, because Car only has a constructor that takes a String.

questions.question: Inside an override of String spec(), a developer writes return spec() + ", 465 km"; instead of super.spec(). What happens at run time?
options: StackOverflowError, because the method keeps calling itself
The parent's spec() runs as intended
questions.explanation: A plain spec() call dispatches to the same override, so it recurses until the stack runs out.

questions.question: class P { String n = "base"; } class Q extends P { String n = "top"; void show() { System.out.println(super.n + " " + n); } } What does new Q().show(); print?
questions.explanation: Q hides P's field. super.n reads P's copy, base, and the plain n reads Q's own copy, top.

questions.question: Can one constructor call both this(...) and super(...)?
options: No, only one of them can be the first statement
questions.explanation: Both calls must be the first statement, so a constructor uses one or the other, never both.

questions.question: A static helper method writes return super.toString(); inside a subclass. Why does it fail?
options: There is no current object in static code, so super cannot be used
questions.explanation: super refers to the parent part of the current object, and a static method has no current object.

questions.question: How can a class reach its grandparent's version of an overridden method?
options: Cast this to the grandparent type and call the method
Not directly; the parent must call super.method() and expose it
questions.explanation: Java has no super.super, and a cast still uses dynamic dispatch. Only the direct parent is reachable with super.
